topic: Why is a negative times a negative a positive?
title: Why Minus Times Minus Is Plus ➕
description:
Ever wondered why multiplying two negatives gives a positive? Let's trace it out step by step using a simple number line. #shorts #maths #education

hook: Why is a negative times a negative a positive?
narration: Why is a negative times a negative a positive? Picture a number line. Walking forward is positive. Walking backward is negative. Now, face backward and walk backward. You end up moving forward. why: Reversing direction twice flips your movement back to the positive side. Try this: what is negative three times positive four?
question: Try this: what is negative three times positive four?
answer_comment: The answer: negative twelve. Walking backward three steps, four times, leaves you twelve steps behind zero on the negative side. One factor is negative, so the final direction stays negative. Drop your questions below!
fact_check: Negative times negative is positive because reversing direction twice points you forward.
Negative three times positive four equals negative twelve.

topic: Why does a transformer only work with alternating current (AC)?
title: Why Transformers Need Changing Current ⚡
description:
Ever wonder why transformers need alternating current to function? Discover how changing magnetic fields make induction work.

#shorts #physics #electronics

Sources (open-access research):
- Gan (2026), Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research). doi:10.5281/zenodo.20597697
- Kumru et al. (2022), European Journal of Science and Technology. doi:10.31590/ejosat.1075985

Board icons: Twemoji by Twitter and contributors, CC BY 4.0
Photo by ds_30 on Pixabay
Photo: unknown, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Video by Cristian-Manieri on Pixabay
hook: Why won't a transformer work with direct current?
narration: Why won't a transformer work with direct current? Connect a battery to the first coil. A steady magnetic field grows, then stops. The second coil feels no change, so no current flows. Switch to alternating current, and the field constantly flips back and forth. Transformers only work with changing magnetic fields, which require a changing current to create. Try this: why does a moving magnet create electricity?
question: Try this: why does a moving magnet create electricity?
answer_comment:
The answer: A moving magnet constantly changes the magnetic field inside the coil. According to Faraday's law, this changing magnetic field induces a voltage in the wire, driving an electric current. It is the exact same changing-field rule that makes transformers work! What happens if you stop moving the magnet?

Sources (open-access research):
- Gan (2026), Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research). doi:10.5281/zenodo.20597697
- Kumru et al. (2022), European Journal of Science and Technology. doi:10.31590/ejosat.1075985

sources.claim: Transformers require a changing magnetic flux to induce voltage in the secondary coil via Faraday's law of induction.
sources.cite: Gan (2026), Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research). doi:10.5281/zenodo.20597697
sources.title: Generators, Motors, and Transformers: How Induction Works
sources.why: It shows how generators convert mechanical motion into electrical energy, how motors convert electrical energy into mechanical motion, and how transformers use changing magnetic flux between coils to change AC voltage levels.

sources.claim: Alternating current continuously changes direction, producing the necessary changing magnetic field.
sources.cite: Kumru et al. (2022), European Journal of Science and Technology. doi:10.31590/ejosat.1075985
sources.title: Numerical Analysis and Comparison of Magnetic Fields Caused by Constant and Time Varying Currents in Medium Voltage Underground Cables
sources.why: However, alternating current, which is the source of the magnetic field, is a time-varying vector quantity.

fact_check: Transformers require a changing magnetic flux to induce voltage in the secondary coil via Faraday's law of induction.
Direct current produces a static magnetic field after initial turn-on, creating zero steady-state induced voltage in the secondary coil.
Alternating current continuously changes direction, producing the necessary changing magnetic field.
Answer to Try this: A moving magnet changes the magnetic flux through the coil, which induces an electromotive force (voltage).

topic: How do vaccines actually train your immune system to fight real viruses?
title: How Vaccines Work: Immune Memory Explained
description:
How do vaccines train your immune system without making you sick? Here is the step-by-step biology of antibodies and memory cells.

#shorts #biology #science

Sources (open-access research):
- Turner et al. (2017), PLoS ONE. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0183877
- Galeone et al. (2024), Viruses. doi:10.3390/v16101515

Photo by whitesession on Pixabay
Video by 4Shaida on Pixabay
Video by Cassiopeia_Arts on Pixabay
hook: You’ve gotten vaccines your whole life, but do you know how they actually train your body?
narration: You’ve gotten vaccines your whole life, but do you know how they actually train your body? Step one: a vaccine introduces harmless viral protein fragments, called antigens, into muscle tissue. Step two: your immune system detects these antigens and builds custom Y-shaped proteins called antibodies to lock onto them. Step three: specialized white blood cells become memory cells, storing the exact shape of that antibody. That's because your body saves molecular blueprints, allowing your immune system to destroy real viruses before you feel sick. This cellular memory is how vaccines successfully eliminated deadly diseases like smallpox worldwide. Try this: why do you need a new flu vaccine almost every year?
question: Try this: why do you need a new flu vaccine almost every year?
answer_comment:
The answer: the influenza virus mutates rapidly, changing the shape of its surface antigens. Because your memory cells look for specific protein shapes, old antibodies cannot recognize the mutated strain. Updated flu vaccines train your immune system to recognize the newest surface shapes!

Sources (open-access research):
- Turner et al. (2017), PLoS ONE. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0183877
- Galeone et al. (2024), Viruses. doi:10.3390/v16101515

sources.claim: Memory B and T cells retain the specific molecular shape of antigens for rapid secondary response.
sources.cite: Turner et al. (2017), PLoS ONE. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0183877
sources.title: Transiently antigen primed B cells can generate multiple subsets of memory cells
sources.why: Memory B cells are long-lived cells that generate a more vigorous response upon recognition of antigen (Ag) and T cell help than naïve B cells and ensure maintenance of durable humoral immunity.

sources.claim: Influenza antigenic drift alters surface hemagglutinin and neuraminidase, requiring annual vaccine reformulations.
sources.title: Evolutionary Insights from Association Rule Mining of Co-Occurring Mutations in Influenza Hemagglutinin and Neuraminidase
sources.why: Seasonal influenza viruses continuously evolve via antigenic drift. This leads to recurring epidemics, globally significant mortality rates, and the need for annually updated vaccines.

fact_check: Vaccines present harmless antigens to stimulate primary antibody production.
Memory B and T cells retain the specific molecular shape of antigens for rapid secondary response.
Immune memory prevents disease onset upon later exposure to the wild pathogen.
Influenza antigenic drift alters surface hemagglutinin and neuraminidase, requiring annual vaccine reformulations.

topic: Why does soap remove grease and oil when plain water cannot?
title: Why Does Soap Remove Grease?
description:
Water alone can't wash away grease, but soap solves this instantly. Discover the molecular bridge that makes cleaning possible.

#chemistry #shorts #science

Video by Kaffeesüchtig on Pixabay
Video by Moos-Media on Pixabay
Video by NickyPe on Pixabay
Video by StefWithAnF on Pixabay
Video by klimkin on Pixabay

How this was made: the script is researched and fact-checked with AI tools against open-access research and textbooks, narrated by an AI voice, and every diagram, number and graph is drawn by code from the real values. Spot a mistake? Tell us in the comments - corrections are checked and credited.
hook: You've used soap your whole life, but do you know how it actually removes grease?
narration: You've used soap your whole life, but do you know how it actually removes grease? Step one: water molecules prefer to stick to each other rather than to greasy surfaces, so they bead up instead of washing the grease away. Step two: a soap molecule has two very different ends. Step three: the long tail grabs the oil, while the head dissolves in water. That's because soap molecules act as an intermediate bridge, linking the polar water to non-polar grease. Try this: why does hot water often help soap clean greasy pans more effectively than cold water?
question: Try this: why does hot water often help soap clean greasy pans more effectively than cold water?
answer_comment: The answer: Hot water gives molecules more kinetic energy, causing them to move faster and melt solid fats into liquids more quickly. This makes it easier for soap molecules to surround and lift the grease away. Additionally, heat lowers the viscosity of the grease, making it flow more easily so soap can break it up. What other everyday items rely on chemistry to clean?
fact_check: Water molecules are polar and do not mix with non-polar grease due to hydrophobic interactions.
Soap molecules possess a polar hydrophilic head and a non-polar hydrophobic tail.
Soap forms micelles around grease, allowing it to be rinsed away by water.
Hot water increases molecular kinetic energy, speeding up the dissolving and melting of fats.
